thread.title: Tech companies sent an ominous message to investors in October

author: Barbara Kollmeyer
title: Tech companies sent an ominous message to investors in October
text:
Getty Images Ominous October Something wicked this way came for investors in October.
Even as another bullish day builds for stocks on All Hallows’ Eve, the damage has been done. The Nasdaq is set for its worst month since October 2008—and the Dow and S&P 500 are looking at the most brutal monthly performances since 2015 and 2010, respectively.
“It has been a wild ride for investors and there is no guarantee it is over yet,” says Craig Erlam, senior market analyst at OANDA, in a note to clients. That’s because next week we’ll get what could be the mother of all midterm election battles, along with a Fed meeting, he says.
See Also Keeping Personal Politics Out of the Classroom, Two Teachers Share Common Ground × Naturally, hard-hit techs are staying in the spotlight, especially with Facebook FB, +2.91% reporting late Tuesday and Apple AAPL, +0.50% ahead for Thursday , and the bar set pretty high these days for companies in general when it comes to earnings reports.
That brings us to our call of the day , from Michael Schoonover, COO and portfolio manager of Catalyst Funds, who has spotted a sign that techs may feel their own companies’ futures are in a bit of trouble. The crux of this can be found via huge drop in tech share buybacks in October, which he lays out in this chart, found in his post on ValueWalk :
The chart shows a decent start for buybacks this year, then a big spike in May as new tax laws kicked in. That allowed for companies to bring back significant amounts of cash from overseas, which they used to buy back shares.
But as of October 26, tech firms announced just $1.7 billion in buybacks, compared with the year-to-date monthly average through September of more than $36 billion for the sector, notes Schoonover.
As he explains, buybacks are rooted in a company’s belief that their stock is undervalued and makes for a better investment opportunity than other options. Investors benefit because those buybacks drive gains for shares.
What’s happening now, he surmises, is that tech companies are finally starting to believe “they will be substantially impacted by the trade war.” No doubt the rhetoric and fears about a U.S./China trade war continue to pepper this market.
“The [buyback] drop is significant not merely in numbers, but also as we enter a period of increased uncertainty. Investors should continue to monitor the buyback activity of technology companies as an indication if the companies continue to see a lack of opportunity in their own stocks,” says Schoonover.

The call The godfather of charts, Ralph Acampora , thinks this boil on markets won’t be lanced soon. “The damage that has been done technically to the stock market is much, much worse than people are talking about,” he told MarketWatch this week, citing the breakdown in so-called FANG stocks .
Jesse Colombo, analyst at Clarity Financial, hits a similar note in our chart of the day:
Colombo’s chart shows the formation of a long-term top for the S&P 500, and harkens back to a blog in February when he discussed the three ways a market correction could play out. The above refers to door #2 and a classic “head and shoulders” pattern, which is seen as a sign of the end of an upward trend .
“If we are indeed following this pattern, the left shoulder was the late-2017 surge and early-2018 plunge, the head was the summer surge and October plunge, and a final “dead cat bounce” would be ahead as the right shoulder forms,” says Colombo, in the post on Real Investment Advice .
In short, the S&P 500 has tracked a trendline higher until it closed below that, a worrying signal for Colombo. “The neckline support level formed at the early-2018 lows and is the key price target that I believe the S&P 500 is going to gun for during the course of this selloff,” he says.
Colombo caused some ripples recently as he warned about an impending massive bubble for stocks linked to household wealth and easy Fed policy.
The buzz Clorox CLX, +2.70% Estée Lauder EL, +3.76% Molson Coors TAP, +2.86% GM GM, +1.24% Sprint S, -1.22% and Kellogg K, +2.23% are on the earnings docket, with AIG AIG, +2.63% Fitbit FIT, +2.08% and Zynga ZNGA, +1.38% due after the close.
An earnings beat and better-than-expected guidance is lifting Facebook FB, +2.91% shares. As for CEO Mark Zuckerberg, he’s done apologizing . Meanwhile, the social media group has begun banning pages linked to far-right extremist group the Proud Boys.

The Basilica, he said , has “aged 20 years in just one day.”
